risks.text: Your site runs a WordPress version that WordPress itself lists as insecure.
Nothing stops scammers from sending email that looks like it came from you.
Browsers aren't told to insist on your secure site, which leaves a gap on public Wi-Fi.

checks.title: Secure connection (HTTPS)
checks.why: Without it, anyone on the same Wi-Fi can read or change what your customers see and type.

checks.title: Sends visitors to the secure version
checks.why: People who type your address without https:// should still land on the secure site.

checks.title: Security certificate is current
checks.why: When it expires, browsers show a full-page warning and most visitors leave.
checks.saw: Expires 20 Dec 2026 · 54 days left · issued by Let's Encrypt

checks.title: Browsers remember to use HTTPS (HSTS)
checks.why: Stops a trick on public Wi-Fi that keeps visitors on the insecure version of your site.

checks.title: No insecure files on the secure page
checks.why: Scripts or images loaded over plain http can be swapped by an attacker, and browsers block some of them.

checks.title: Forms send securely
checks.why: Anything typed into a form that posts over plain http can be read along the way, and browsers warn people before sending it.

checks.title: The www address works too
checks.why: Plenty of people still type www. If that version is broken or shows a security warning, they think your whole site is.

checks.title: Can't be hidden inside another site
checks.why: Stops scam pages from loading your site invisibly and tricking people into clicking your buttons.

checks.title: Files can't pretend to be scripts (nosniff)
checks.why: Stops browsers from running a file as code when it claims to be something else.

checks.title: Content Security Policy
checks.why: A list of where your site's scripts may come from. If bad code sneaks in, the browser refuses to run it.

checks.title: Page addresses stay private (Referrer-Policy)
checks.why: Controls how much of your page address is shared when a visitor clicks a link to another site.
checks.saw: Not set, so browsers use their safe default (strict-origin-when-cross-origin).

checks.title: Camera, mic and location locked (Permissions-Policy)
checks.why: Makes sure nothing embedded in your site can ask visitors for their camera, microphone or location.

checks.title: Cookies are protected
checks.why: Cookies can hold logins and carts. The Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite flags keep them from being stolen.

checks.title: Doesn't advertise software versions
checks.why: Showing exact versions (like 'Apache 2.4.41') tells attackers which known holes to try.
checks.saw: Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu) · X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.3 · page says it was made with WordPress 6.4.2

checks.title: Email sender list (SPF)
checks.why: Tells inboxes which servers may send email as your domain. Without it, scammers can send fake invoices that look like yours.

checks.title: Email spoofing protection (DMARC)
checks.why: Tells inboxes what to do with fake email that uses your domain: let it in, send it to junk, or reject it.

checks.title: Email signing (DKIM)
checks.why: A signature that proves your email really came from you. Not scored, because DKIM keys can be named anything and we can only look in the usual places.
checks.saw: Found a signing key at google._domainkey.joesbakery.example.

checks.title: Not flagged as dangerous
checks.why: Security filters block sites known for malware or scams. A hacked site can end up there without its owner ever finding out.
checks.saw: Not blocked by Cloudflare or Quad9's malware filters.

checks.title: No known-risky software versions
checks.why: Old versions of WordPress and common code libraries have published security holes that attackers scan for.
checks.saw: WordPress 6.4.2: WordPress lists this version as insecure · jQuery 1.12.4 (cross-site scripting holes, CVE-2020-11022 and CVE-2020-11023)

checks.title: Domain name isn't about to expire
checks.why: If your domain lapses, your site and email stop working, and someone else can buy the name.
checks.saw: Paid through 14 Feb 2027 · 109 days left · registrar: GoDaddy.com, LLC

checks.title: Domain is locked against transfers
checks.why: A transfer lock stops anyone who gets into your account, or fools your registrar, from quietly moving your domain away.

checks.title: Other companies' code on your homepage
checks.why: Scripts from other companies can read what people type on your page. Not scored, because most sites need some, but you should know who is on the list.
checks.saw: 2 companies: Google Tag Manager, Meta (Facebook). Tag managers can load more than this list shows.

fixes.title: Add a DMARC record
fixes.text: Add this TXT record. It sends fake email that uses your domain to junk. If you send a lot of email, start with p=none for two weeks, then switch to quarantine.

fixes.title: Add the missing security headers
fixes.text: Add these headers to every page. The Content-Security-Policy line is a safe starter that can't break your scripts. It won't raise your score by itself: a policy that limits scripts needs testing on your site first.
fixes.code:
<IfModule mod_headers.c>
  Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000"
  Header always set X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN"
  Header always set Content-Security-Policy "upgrade-insecure-requests; frame-ancestors 'self'"
  Header always set Permissions-Policy "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()"
</IfModule>

fixes.title: Update WordPress
fixes.text: Back up the site, then open Dashboard → Updates and update WordPress, your plugins and your theme. Turn on automatic updates so this stays fixed.

fixes.title: Flag your cookies
fixes.text: Ask whoever set up your site (or check your plugin settings) to add the missing flags. Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax suit most cookies.

fixes.title: Hide version numbers (and keep that software updated)
fixes.text: Remove the WordPress version tag with a security plugin, or add this to your theme's functions.php. Then keep WordPress and its plugins updated.
